final_text: PostgreSQL does not check for deadlock on every lock: a waiting transaction first sleeps for deadlock_timeout (default 1 second), and only then runs the relatively expensive deadlock check.
note: PG 18 runtime-config-locks: deadlock_timeout is 'the amount of time to wait on a lock before checking to see if there is a deadlock condition. The check for deadlock is relatively expensive'; 'The default is one second (1s)'.

final_text: InnoDB picks the victim by size: it 'tries to pick small transactions to roll back', measured by rows inserted, updated or deleted. The victim gets ERROR 1213 and its whole transaction is rolled back; the application should retry the entire transaction.
note: MySQL 8.4 deadlock-detection: 'InnoDB tries to pick small transactions to roll back, where the size of a transaction is determined by the number of rows inserted, updated, or deleted.' Error-handling page: a deadlock 'causes InnoDB to roll back the entire transaction. Retry the entire transaction'. ERROR 1213 is shown on the deadlock-example page.

final_text: Oracle breaks a deadlock by rolling back only one statement (of the transaction that detects it), not the whole transaction; the application should then roll back explicitly or retry.
note: Oracle 19c Concepts: resolves deadlocks 'by rolling back one statement involved in the deadlock'; 'The statement rolled back belongs to the transaction that detects the deadlock. Usually, the signaled transaction should be rolled back explicitly, but it can retry the rolled-back statement'.

final_text: The standard defence: make every code path acquire locks on multiple rows in the same order (for example, ascending primary key). Two transactions that lock rows in the same order cannot form a cycle.
note: PG explicit-locking: 'The best defense against deadlocks is generally to avoid them by being certain that all applications using a database acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order.' Its example notes that same-order updates would not have deadlocked.

final_text: Under MVCC an exclusive row lock does not block ordinary SELECTs: they read the last committed version, and only other writers and locking reads (FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE) wait. The exception is InnoDB at SERIALIZABLE with autocommit off, where plain SELECTs become SELECT ... FOR SHARE and do wait.
note: MySQL locking-reads: 'Consistent reads ignore any locks set on the records'; PG: 'Row-level locks do not affect data querying; they block only writers and lockers to the same row.' Reworded to add the documented InnoDB SERIALIZABLE exception (plain SELECTs become FOR SHARE when autocommit is off, per innodb-transaction-isolation-levels), so the sentence is not an absolute.

final_text: Lock upgrade is a classic deadlock source: if two transactions both hold a shared lock on the same row and both then try to update it, each waits for the other's S lock, and InnoDB rolls one back. MySQL's own deadlock example is a close variant: each client holds an S lock on one row, then tries to update the row the other has share-locked.
note: The MySQL 8.4 deadlock example is not the same-row upgrade: client A holds an S lock on Animals 'Aardvark', client B an S lock on Birds 'Buzzard', then each UPDATEs the row the other holds ('ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found'). The same-row case follows from the compatibility rules on innodb-locking ('A request by T2 for an X lock cannot be granted immediately' while T1 holds S). Reworded so the manual is not mis-cited.

final_text: SKIP LOCKED returns 'an inconsistent view of the data', so both MySQL and PostgreSQL say it is not for general transactional work. It is meant for queue-like tables where any free row will do, like job queues or seat/coupon pools.
note: MySQL: 'Queries that skip locked rows return an inconsistent view of the data. SKIP LOCKED is therefore not suitable for general transactional work' ... 'queue-like table'. PG: 'Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work'. Paraphrase is fair for both.

final_text: In MySQL 8.0+, SELECT ... FOR SHARE replaces the older SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE, which still works for backward compatibility. Unlike the old form, FOR SHARE accepts the OF table_name, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED options (FOR UPDATE accepts them too).
note: MySQL locking-reads: 'SELECT ... FOR SHARE is a replacement for SELECT ... LOCK IN SHARE MODE, but LOCK IN SHARE MODE remains available for backward compatibility ... However, FOR SHARE supports OF table_name, NOWAIT, and SKIP LOCKED options.' The page also says NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED 'may be used with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or SELECT ... FOR SHARE', so 'Only FOR SHARE supports' was misleading.

final_text: Real defaults: InnoDB waits innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 50 seconds for a row lock; PostgreSQL's lock_timeout defaults to 0, which means wait indefinitely unless you set it.
note: MySQL 8.4 innodb-parameters: innodb_lock_wait_timeout 'The default value is 50 seconds.' PG runtime-config-client: lock_timeout 'A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout.'

final_text: After a lock wait timeout, MySQL rolls back only the waiting statement, not the whole transaction (unless --innodb-rollback-on-timeout is set). The transaction stays open and still holds its earlier locks, so the code should roll back or retry.
note: MySQL error-handling: 'A lock wait timeout causes InnoDB to roll back the current statement ... To have the entire transaction roll back, start the server with --innodb-rollback-on-timeout enabled.' That locks taken earlier stay held is the consequence of the transaction not being rolled back (inference, not a quoted sentence).

final_text: In PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED, a waiter re-evaluates its WHERE clause against the updated version of the row and skips it if it no longer matches. At REPEATABLE READ the waiter instead fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' and must retry.
note: PG 18 transaction-iso: Read Committed waiter 'will attempt to apply its operation to the updated version of the row. The search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated'; Repeatable Read: 'ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update'.

final_text: Indexes matter for locking: in InnoDB a locking read or UPDATE locks every index record it scans, whatever the WHERE clause says. Without a suitable index (for example on trip_id, user_id) it may lock every row of the table.
note: MySQL innodb-locks-set: locking reads, UPDATE and DELETE 'set record locks on every index record that is scanned ... It does not matter whether there are WHERE conditions'; without a suitable index 'every row of the table becomes locked'.

final_text: Which waiter gets a contended InnoDB lock is decided by Contention-Aware Transaction Scheduling (CATS). The transaction blocking the most others goes first; ties go to the longest-waiting transaction.
note: MySQL innodb-transaction-scheduling: CATS weight is 'based on the number of transactions that a transaction blocks ... If weights are equal, priority is given to the longest waiting transaction.' Useful but engine-internal.

final_text: A single 'UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1 WHERE id = ?' does not lose updates: the UPDATE locks the row and a concurrent updater waits. At READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL's default) the waiter then applies its change to the updated row; at REPEATABLE READ PostgreSQL aborts it with a serialization error to retry. Lost updates come from reading the value into the application and writing it back.
note: PG 18 transaction-iso supports the READ COMMITTED behaviour (waiter applies 'its operation to the updated version of the row'), but at REPEATABLE READ the second updater fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. The original wording held only for READ COMMITTED; reworded to state the condition.

final_text: In MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ, all plain SELECTs in a transaction see the snapshot taken at its first read. A transaction that has already read will not see later commits until it commits and starts again.
note: MySQL innodb-consistent-read: 'all consistent reads within the same transaction read the snapshot established by the first such read in that transaction. You can get a fresher snapshot ... by committing the current transaction'.

final_text: PostgreSQL has four row-lock strengths: FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE. The weaker modes conflict less: for example, FOR NO KEY UPDATE does not block FOR KEY SHARE on the same row.
note: PG explicit-locking lists FOR UPDATE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR KEY SHARE and says FOR NO KEY UPDATE 'will not block SELECT FOR KEY SHARE'. The foreign-key example is not on the page I opened, so it was replaced by what the page says.

final_text: On very high-concurrency InnoDB systems, deadlock detection itself can slow things down when many threads wait on the same lock. MySQL lets you disable it (innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF) and rely on innodb_lock_wait_timeout instead.
note: MySQL deadlock-detection: 'On high concurrency systems, deadlock detection can cause a slowdown when numerous threads wait for the same lock ... rely on the innodb_lock_wait_timeout setting' and 'can be disabled using the innodb_deadlock_detect variable'.

final_text: In PostgreSQL any error, including a NOWAIT lock failure, puts the whole transaction block into an aborted state. Only ROLLBACK, or ROLLBACK TO a savepoint taken before the failing statement, recovers it.
note: PG tutorial-transactions: 'ROLLBACK TO is the only way to regain control of a transaction block that was put in aborted state by the system due to an error, short of rolling it back completely'. sql-select: with NOWAIT 'the statement reports an error'. Combined, the addition holds.

final_text: PostgreSQL keeps no in-memory list of locked rows: it marks the lock in the row itself, so SELECT FOR UPDATE can cause disk writes. As a result there is no limit on how many rows can be locked at once.
note: PG explicit-locking: 'PostgreSQL doesn't remember any information about modified rows in memory, so there is no limit on the number of rows locked at one time. However, locking a row might cause a disk write'.

final_text: PostgreSQL warns that at READ COMMITTED a SELECT with ORDER BY and a locking clause can return rows out of order: it sorts first, then may block while locking. With LIMIT, locking stops once enough rows have been returned.
note: PG sql-select Caution: a SELECT at READ COMMITTED 'using ORDER BY and a locking clause' may 'return rows out of order' because it sorts first and then may block; 'If a LIMIT is used, locking stops once enough rows have been returned'.

final_text: Defaults differ by database: MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, while PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED. Neither defaults to SERIALIZABLE.
note: MySQL: 'The default isolation level for InnoDB is REPEATABLE READ.' PG 18: 'Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL.'

final_text: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE does not queue transactions. It runs them concurrently and aborts one with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001) when the result could differ from a serial order, so applications 'must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures'.
note: PG 18 transaction-iso: SSI monitoring 'does not introduce any blocking beyond that present in repeatable read'; 'must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures' (quote verbatim); failures 'always return with an SQLSTATE value of 40001'.

final_text: In MySQL InnoDB, SERIALIZABLE is REPEATABLE READ plus one change: plain SELECTs are implicitly turned into SELECT ... FOR SHARE when autocommit is disabled. Two transactions that both read a seat and then try to update it can therefore deadlock.
note: MySQL isolation-levels: SERIALIZABLE 'is like REPEATABLE READ, but InnoDB implicitly converts all plain SELECT statements to SELECT ... FOR SHARE if autocommit is disabled.' The deadlock consequence follows from S-then-X on the same row.

final_text: MySQL defines SELECT ... FOR UPDATE as locking rows 'the same as if you issued an UPDATE statement for those rows'. An UPDATE ... WHERE sets an exclusive lock on every record its search encounters, so an UPDATE is always a locking operation.
note: MySQL locking-reads: 'the same as if you issued an UPDATE statement for those rows'; locks-set: 'UPDATE ... WHERE ... sets an exclusive next-key lock on every record the search encounters'. Both verbatim.

final_text: In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, a second UPDATE of a row that another transaction is updating waits for it to commit, then re-checks its WHERE clause against the new row version before applying. Under REPEATABLE READ the same situation aborts with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update', and the transaction must be retried.
note: PG 18 transaction-iso: Read Committed waiter re-evaluates the WHERE clause on the updated version; Repeatable Read gives 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'.

final_text: PostgreSQL warns that 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.' This is why deep pages of LIMIT/OFFSET pagination get slower and keyset (cursor) pagination is preferred.
note: PG queries-limit: quote verbatim. The keyset-pagination clause is reasoning, not on the page, but follows directly from the quoted sentence.

final_text: MySQL stops early on LIMIT when it can: with ORDER BY on an index it reads only the first rows, but if a filesort is needed, 'all rows that match the query without the LIMIT clause are selected, and most or all of them are sorted' before the first rows are returned.
note: MySQL limit-optimization: 'If ordering is done by using an index, this is very fast. If a filesort must be done, all rows that match the query without the LIMIT clause are selected, and most or all of them are sorted, before the first row_count are found.' Quote verbatim.

final_text: In MySQL, what is flushed at commit is the redo log. With the default innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, 'Logs are written and flushed to disk at each transaction commit'. Settings 0 and 2 flush about once per second, and unflushed transactions 'can be lost in a crash'.
note: MySQL 8.4 innodb-parameters: 'The default setting of 1 is required for full ACID compliance. Logs are written and flushed to disk at each transaction commit.' Settings 0 and 2 flush 'once per second'; unflushed transactions 'can be lost in a crash'.

final_text: InnoDB 'does not physically remove a row from the database immediately when you delete it'. The row is delete-marked and later physically removed by a background purge, once no transaction needs it for MVCC or rollback.
note: MySQL purge-configuration: 'InnoDB does not physically remove a row from the database immediately when you delete it'; removal 'only occurs after the row is no longer required for multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) or rollback, is called a purge'.

final_text: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE or DELETE leaves the old row version in place because it 'must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions'. VACUUM later removes these dead row versions and marks the space for reuse.
note: PG routine-vacuuming 24.1.2: old version 'must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions'; 'VACUUM removes dead row versions in tables and indexes and marks the space available for future reuse'.

final_text: DynamoDB's TTL feature deletes expired items in the background, 'typically within a few days after their expiration', without consuming write throughput. Until then expired items can still be returned, so queries should filter them out.
note: DynamoDB TTL page: 'deletes expired items within a few days of their expiration time, without consuming write throughput'; 'typically within a few days after their expiration' (verbatim); 'Use filter expressions to remove expired items from Scan and Query results.'

final_text: System-versioned temporal tables (SQL Server 2016 and later, Azure SQL) give opt-in, built-in history: on DELETE 'The system stores the previous value of the row in the history table', and the row vanishes from normal queries but can still be read with FOR SYSTEM_TIME.
note: Microsoft Learn temporal-tables (updated 2026-08-18, applies to SQL Server 2016+): Deletes - 'The system stores the previous value of the row in the history table ... In the current table, the row is removed'; queried with FOR SYSTEM_TIME. The page does not mention SQL:2011, so that label was dropped.

final_text: The building blocks named here have sharp edges. MySQL says SKIP LOCKED queries 'return an inconsistent view of the data' and are 'not suitable for general transactional work', but they suit queue-like tables. NOWAIT fails immediately with an error instead of waiting for a locked row.
note: MySQL locking-reads: SKIP LOCKED 'return an inconsistent view of the data' and 'not suitable for general transactional work'; NOWAIT 'failing with an error if a requested row is locked'. Overlaps A-C-07 and A-KSD-18; keep only one on the page.

final_text: Django's CONN_MAX_AGE defaults to 0, which closes the database connection at the end of each request. Native connection pooling for PostgreSQL (OPTIONS 'pool' with psycopg) only arrived in Django 5.1.
note: Django 5.2 databases: CONN_MAX_AGE 'The default value is 0, preserving the historical behavior of closing the database connection at the end of each request'; Connection pool 'New in Django 5.1', OPTIONS 'pool' with psycopg.

final_text: Not every ORM is weak at pooling: SQLAlchemy's Engine 'has a QueuePool integrated, pre-configured with reasonable pooling defaults' (pool size 5).
note: SQLAlchemy 2.0 pooling: the Engine 'has a QueuePool integrated, pre-configured with reasonable pooling defaults'; default 'QueuePool of size five' (max_overflow 10).

final_text: Django lets you load only some columns: only() loads just the named fields and defer() skips the named ones (a deferred field is fetched on first access, one query per field). values() returns plain dicts instead of model instances.
note: Django querysets: defer() fields are retrieved 'if you access that field (one at a time, not all the deferred fields at once)'; only() loads just the named fields; values() 'returns dictionaries, rather than model instances'.

final_text: A classic ORM performance trap is the N+1 query pattern, where touching a related object in a loop fires one query per row. Django's select_related (a JOIN) and prefetch_related (one batched query) are 'designed to stop the deluge of database queries that is caused by accessing related objects'.
note: Django querysets (prefetch_related): 'both are designed to stop the deluge of database queries that is caused by accessing related objects' - verbatim.

final_text: Django can call a stored procedure directly with cursor.callproc(name, params), and can map raw SQL results onto model instances with Manager.raw().
note: Django topics/db/sql: callproc 'Calls a database stored procedure with the given name' with params; raw() 'automatically maps fields in the query to fields on the model'.

final_text: Vitess is 'an open-source database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL' through sharding, and it 'served all YouTube database traffic for over five years'.
note: vitess.io: 'an open-source database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL'; 'Vitess served all YouTube database traffic for over five years.' Both verbatim.

final_text: In E. F. Codd's relational model a relation is 'a set of tuples', each element drawn from a data domain. In SQL, relations are 'represented by tables', and each row represents one tuple.
note: Wikipedia Relation (database): Codd's relation is 'a set of tuples' with each element from a data domain; in SQL relations are 'represented by tables' and each row 'represents a single tuple'. 'In its mathematical sense' is not on the page I read, so it was removed.

final_text: In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, and every secondary-index record also stores the primary-key columns. A long key therefore also bloats the expired_at index: MySQL notes 'it is advantageous to have a short primary key'.
note: MySQL innodb-index-types: 'each record in a secondary index contains the primary key columns'; 'If the primary key is long, the secondary indexes use more space, so it is advantageous to have a short primary key.'

final_text: MySQL BLOB size classes: TINYBLOB < 256 B, BLOB < 64 KB, MEDIUMBLOB < 16 MB, LONGBLOB < 4 GB. A value column meant to hold multi-megabyte objects must be MEDIUMBLOB or LONGBLOB.
note: MySQL storage-requirements: TINYBLOB L < 2^8, BLOB L < 2^16, MEDIUMBLOB L < 2^24, LONGBLOB L < 2^32 bytes - matches the sizes given.

final_text: PostgreSQL upsert syntax: INSERT INTO store (key, value, expired_at) VALUES ($1, $2, $3) ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value, expired_at = EXCLUDED.expired_at; EXCLUDED refers to the row that was proposed for insertion.
note: PG sql-insert: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE; 'the row proposed for insertion using the special excluded table'; 'This is also known as UPSERT'. No UPSERT keyword exists.

final_text: MySQL REPLACE INTO deletes the existing row and inserts a new one ('It either inserts, or deletes and inserts'). INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE modifies the existing row in place. For a put that replaces a value, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE avoids the extra delete.
note: MySQL replace: 'It either inserts, or deletes and inserts' (verbatim); ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE 'either inserts or updates'. The page notes an engine may internally do the REPLACE as an update 'but the semantics are the same'.

final_text: Get-then-insert is also racy: two concurrent puts can both see 'key absent' and one INSERT then fails on the primary key. PostgreSQL documents that ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE yields an atomic insert-or-update outcome 'even under high concurrency'.
note: PG sql-insert: 'ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE guarantees an atomic INSERT or UPDATE outcome; provided there is no independent error, one of those two outcomes is guaranteed, even under high concurrency.'

final_text: Redis uses the same idea: 'Keys expiring information is stored as absolute Unix timestamps (in milliseconds in case of Redis version 2.6 or greater)'. Because of that, expiry depends on a stable system clock.
note: redis.io EXPIRE appendix: 'Keys expiring information is stored as absolute Unix timestamps (in milliseconds in case of Redis version 2.6 or greater)' (verbatim); 'For expires to work well, the computer time must be taken stable.'

final_text: For a large backlog, run the cleanup in chunks: MySQL's DELETE ... LIMIT row_count caps rows per statement, and you repeat the DELETE until fewer rows than the limit are affected. That keeps each statement short.
note: MySQL delete: 'the MySQL-specific LIMIT row_count clause for DELETE specifies the maximum number of rows to be deleted. If the number of rows to delete is larger than the limit, repeat the DELETE statement until the number of affected rows is less than the LIMIT value.'

final_text: If 'no TTL' is stored as NULL, comparisons like ttl > NOW() return NULL, so such rows never match. Use a far-future sentinel for 'no expiry', or write (ttl IS NULL OR ttl > NOW()) in GET and the user-delete UPDATE.
note: MySQL working-with-null: 'the result of any arithmetic comparison with NULL is also NULL'; PG functions-comparison: 'Ordinary comparison operators yield null ... when either input is null.'

final_text: MySQL TIMESTAMP only covers '1970-01-01 00:00:01' to '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC. For an expiry column use DATETIME (to 9999-12-31) or an integer epoch, which also allows a -1 marker.
note: MySQL datetime: 'TIMESTAMP has a range of 1970-01-01 00:00:01 UTC to 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC'; DATETIME '1000-01-01 00:00:00' to '9999-12-31 23:59:59'. The -1 marker point is reasoning.

final_text: InnoDB does not physically remove a deleted row at once: it is removed by a background purge after it is no longer needed for MVCC or rollback. Index pages are merged only when they fall below MERGE_THRESHOLD (default 50% full).
note: MySQL purge-configuration (physical removal by purge after no longer needed for MVCC/rollback) and index-page-merge-threshold ('The default MERGE_THRESHOLD value is 50').

final_text: Redis 6.0 rewrote the active expire cycle and made it tunable: active-expire-effort (1-10, default 1) trades CPU for fewer leftover expired keys. At the default, Redis tries to keep under about 10% of expired keys in memory.
note: Redis 6.0 RC1 release notes (19 Dec 2019): 'The Redis active expire cycle was rewritten for much faster eviction of keys that are already expired. Now the effort is tunable.' redis.conf (unstable): active-expire-effort 1-10, default 1, will 'try to avoid having more than ten percent of expired keys still in memory'.

final_text: Deleting a big key with DEL blocks Redis's main thread, 'even seconds' for large objects. UNLINK removes the key at once and frees its memory on a background thread. The lazyfree-lazy-* options (eviction, expire, server-del, user-del) do the same for those paths, but all are off by default.
note: redis.conf (unstable): DEL of a big value can block 'for a long time (even seconds)'; 'UNLINK (non blocking DEL)'; lazyfree-lazy-eviction/expire/server-del/user-del all default 'no'. Reworded to say these options are off by default.

final_text: RFC 6455 has Ping and Pong control frames. 'A Ping frame may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive', and the peer must answer with a Pong.
note: RFC 6455 5.5.2: 'A Ping frame may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive' and 'an endpoint MUST send a Pong frame in response, unless it already received a Close frame'.

final_text: MySQL JSON columns are not indexed directly. To query a field inside the JSON fast, index a generated column that extracts it; InnoDB also supports multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays.
note: MySQL json: 'JSON columns, like columns of other binary types, are not indexed directly; instead, you can create an index on a generated column'; 'The InnoDB storage engine supports multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays.'

final_text: Both MySQL ('Replication is asynchronous by default') and PostgreSQL streaming replication are asynchronous by default. That small delay is what makes replica reads possibly stale; both offer synchronous or semi-synchronous modes at a latency cost.
note: MySQL replication: 'Replication is asynchronous by default' (verbatim), semisynchronous supported. PG warm-standby: 'Streaming replication is asynchronous by default ... small delay between committing a transaction in the primary and the changes becoming visible in the standby'; synchronous replication available.

final_text: Cross-partition ACID is possible but costs more: DynamoDB's TransactWriteItems commits up to 100 items all-or-nothing, but performs two underlying writes per item (prepare and commit) and cancels on conflicts.
note: DynamoDB transaction-apis: TransactWriteItems 'groups up to 100 write actions in a single all-or-nothing operation'; 'two underlying reads or writes of every item ... one to prepare the transaction and one to commit'; conflicts fail with TransactionCanceledException. Same account and Region only.

final_text: Ignite's links to relational databases are optional: it can act as a caching layer over an RDBMS through CacheStore implementations such as CacheJdbcPojoStore (read-through on cache misses, write-through on updates), and Ignite 2's default SQL engine uses the H2 database to parse and plan queries. Its data storage is its own.
note: Ignite 2.18 external-storage: 'You can use Ignite as a caching layer on top of an existing database such as an RDBMS'; CacheJdbcPojoStore; read-through/write-through definitions confirmed. I also opened the Ignite 2 SQL introduction: 'Ignite's default SQL engine uses H2 Database to parse and optimize queries and generate execution plans' - a second, likely source of the 'built on a relational DB' impression, added to the text.

final_text: MySQL warns that SKIP LOCKED returns an inconsistent view and is 'not suitable for general transactional work'; it fits queue-like tables. NOWAIT instead fails immediately with an error when the row is locked.
note: MySQL locking-reads: quotes verbatim ('not suitable for general transactional work', NOWAIT fails with an error). Duplicates A-C-07 / A-DL-13; show once.

final_text: In MySQL, growing a VARCHAR can be done in place only while the length prefix stays the same size (0-255 bytes, or 256+ bytes). Crossing 255 bytes, or changing the data type, needs a full table copy.
note: MySQL online-DDL: in-place only 'from 0 to 255 bytes, or from 256 bytes to a greater size'; crossing needs ALGORITHM=COPY; 'Changing the column data type is only supported with ALGORITHM=COPY.' Note the limit is in bytes (utf8mb4 = up to 4 bytes per character).

final_text: Go goroutines start with small stacks that grow as needed, and the runtime multiplexes them onto multiple OS threads, so a goroutine blocked on I/O does not stall the others.
note: Effective Go: 'the stacks start small, so they are cheap, and grow by allocating (and freeing) heap storage as required'; 'Goroutines are multiplexed onto multiple OS threads so if one should block, such as while waiting for I/O, others continue to run.' (Document dates from Go's 2009 release; statement still holds.)
